body:
From handwritten manuscripts to printed texts

India had a long tradition of handwritten manuscripts in Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian and various regional languages. Manuscripts could preserve and transmit knowledge, but preparing multiple copies by hand was generally slow and expensive.

The printing press made it easier to produce many copies of a text. As printing developed and distribution widened, books, pamphlets, journals and newspapers could reach more readers.

Printing did not immediately make everyone literate. However, the availability of cheaper printed material helped create new forms of communication and public discussion.

Early printing and newspapers in India

Printing presses were introduced to Goa by Portuguese missionaries in the mid-16th century. Missionary printing subsequently contributed to the production of religious and educational material in Indian languages.

In 1780, James Augustus Hicky began publishing Hicky's Bengal Gazette in Calcutta. It is conventionally identified as the first newspaper printed in India. It was an English-language weekly and became known for criticism of East India Company officials.

Hicky's publication demonstrates that early press conflicts were not confined to Indian-language journalism. European publishers could also face government pressure when their writing challenged colonial authorities.

Missionary activity expanded printing in the following period. A press was established at Serampore in 1800, and Serampore College was established in 1818.

What was the public sphere?

Public sphere: The space in which people exchange information, discuss matters of common concern, criticise policies and express opinions beyond their private households. In colonial India, newspapers, pamphlets, associations and public meetings helped create such spaces.

The public sphere was not a single building or institution. It included the activities through which opinions could become known to a wider audience.

For example, a newspaper could publish criticism of a government policy. Readers could discuss the article, circulate it to others, raise the issue in an association and submit a petition demanding change. A local complaint could thus become part of a wider public debate.

Print capitalism and the circulation of ideas

Print capitalism describes the commercial production and sale of printed material. Printers and publishers depended on readers, subscriptions, advertisements and markets for their publications.

Producing multiple copies made it possible to circulate the same information among people who did not personally know one another. Publications in a common language helped readers become familiar with events and concerns beyond their immediate locality.

This contributed to the spread of shared political awareness. Nevertheless, readers did not necessarily accept the same interpretation of what they read, and publications could express opposing views.

Print and social reform

Printed pamphlets and newspapers enabled reformers to criticise practices relating to caste, religion and the condition of women. Supporters of existing practices could also publish replies. Print therefore widened debate rather than producing agreement automatically.

Women increasingly appeared as readers and writers, especially where education became available. Printed texts also helped spread arguments against caste discrimination. Yet the size and composition of the reading public remained limited by unequal access to literacy.

Information could travel beyond the number of people who personally bought a newspaper because its contents could be read aloud and discussed in public places.

Prelims focus

  • Printing presses reached Goa with Portuguese missionaries in the mid-16th century.
  • Hicky's Bengal Gazette began publication in 1780.
  • James Augustus Hicky was associated with early English-language journalism in Calcutta.
  • A printing press was established at Serampore in 1800.
  • Serampore College was established in 1818.
  • Trap: The introduction of printing presses and the establishment of the first newspaper were different events.

[NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, chapter Print Culture and the Modern World, sections India and the World of Print, Religious Reform and Public Debates and Women and Print, printed pp. 167–174; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, chapter 7, printed p. 86, and chapter 8, printed pp. 95–96.]

title: Printing, Newspapers and the Emergence of a Public Sphere in Colonial India

body:
Why newspapers became important

Newspapers provided information about government decisions, social controversies, trade, public events and conditions in different regions. Indian editors and writers increasingly used them to criticise colonial policies and express demands for reform.

Both English-language newspapers and vernacular newspapers contributed to public opinion. English newspapers could reach an influential educated readership, including some British officials, while publications in Indian languages could address people more familiar with regional languages.

The language of publication is therefore an important fact when studying the history of the Indian press.

Major newspapers and their associations

NewspaperYearLanguagePerson or distinguishing fact
Hicky's Bengal Gazette1780EnglishJames Augustus Hicky; Calcutta
Sambad Kaumudi1821BengaliAssociated with Raja Rammohun Roy and social reform
Samachar Chandrika1822BengaliExpressed orthodox opposition to reformist arguments
Bombay Samachar1822GujaratiFounded by Fardunjee Marzban in Bombay
Vartaman1849GujaratiPublished in connection with the Gujarat Vernacular Society
Amrita Bazar Patrika1868Initially BengaliChanged to English-only publication in 1878
The Hindu1878EnglishFounded in Madras; associated with G. Subramania Aiyer and M. Veeraraghavachariar
Kesari1881MarathiAssociated with Bal Gangadhar Tilak
The Mahratta1881EnglishAssociated with Bal Gangadhar Tilak

These newspapers did not share the same political or social views. Sambad Kaumudi supported reformist arguments associated with Rammohun Roy, while Samachar Chandrika represented opposition to some of those arguments. Newspapers could therefore become platforms for disagreement within Indian society, not merely opposition to British rule.

Gujarat connection: Bombay Samachar

Bombay Samachar began publication in 1822 through the efforts of Fardunjee Marzban. It became an important early Gujarati newspaper associated with Bombay's commercial and Gujarati-speaking communities.

Its history illustrates that Gujarati print culture developed not only within the geographical territory of present-day Gujarat, but also in Bombay, where Gujarati merchants and other communities were active.

Gujarat Vernacular Society, Ahmedabad

The Gujarat Vernacular Society was founded in Ahmedabad on 26 December 1848 through the initiative of British official Alexander Kinloch Forbes. Gujarati literary figures, especially Dalpatram, became closely associated with its activities.

The society promoted Gujarati language, literature and education. Its work included publications, a library and support for girls' education.

  • 1848: Gujarat Vernacular Society established in Ahmedabad.
  • 1849: The society began publishing the Gujarati newspaper Vartaman.
  • 1854: Buddhiprakash was issued as a regular monthly journal associated with the society. Its origins as a periodical predated this monthly phase.

The society demonstrates how vernacular publishing and educational activity could develop together. The availability of books and periodicals encouraged reading, while schools and literary organisations helped create readers and writers.

The Gujarat Vernacular Society was primarily a literary and educational organisation. It should not be treated as identical in purpose to the later political associations that organised demands for Indian representation in government.

Two newspaper pairs worth distinguishing

Kesari and The Mahratta were both associated with Bal Gangadhar Tilak, but the former was published in Marathi and the latter in English.

Amrita Bazar Patrika was founded before the Vernacular Press Act. Its important association with 1878 is the change to English-only publication following the enactment of that law, not the newspaper's original establishment.

Prelims focus

  • Sambad Kaumudi: 1821, associated with Raja Rammohun Roy.
  • Bombay Samachar: 1822, Gujarati, founded by Fardunjee Marzban.
  • Gujarat Vernacular Society: 1848, Ahmedabad, associated with A. K. Forbes and Dalpatram.
  • Vartaman: Gujarati newspaper begun in 1849.
  • Kesari: Marathi; The Mahratta: English.
  • Trap: Amrita Bazar Patrika began in 1868; it changed to English-only publication in 1878.

[NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, chapter Print Culture and the Modern World, printed pp. 168–170 and 175; NCERT, Understanding Society, Class 12 Sociology, chapter Mass Media and Communications, discussion of the early Indian press, 2025–26 reprint; The Indian Express, Know Your City: A Harbinger of Change, How Gujarat Vernacular Society Shaped Ahmedabad, 31 December 2023, consulted 20 November 2026; The Hindu Group, Our Legacy, entry dated 20 September 1878, consulted 20 November 2026; German Specialist Information Service for South Asia, Amrita Bazar Patrika, historical collection description, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Gujarati print culture developed through connected centres in Bombay and Ahmedabad.

title: Important Newspapers and Gujarat's Vernacular Public Life

body:
Why did the colonial government regulate newspapers?

The British authorities recognised that newspapers could influence public opinion and expose government policies to criticism. The colonial state introduced different kinds of press regulations to identify publishers, supervise newspapers, restrict criticism or punish publications considered threatening.

These measures did not all serve the same purpose. Some required registration and declarations, while others imposed licensing, censorship, financial securities or confiscation. Distinguishing the provisions is more useful than remembering dates alone.

Important press regulations

YearMeasureAssociated authorityMain feature
1799Press restrictionsLord WellesleyRestrictions including pre-publication scrutiny
1823Press RegulationsJohn AdamLicensing requirements for printing presses
1835Metcalfe's Press ActCharles MetcalfeRemoved earlier licensing restrictions, with declarations required
1857Temporary press licensing measuresLord CanningTighter control during the rebellion
1867Press and Registration of Books ActBritish Indian governmentDeclarations and registration of printing and publications
1878Vernacular Press ActLord LyttonSpecial restrictions on non-English newspapers
1882Repeal of the Vernacular Press ActLord RiponEnded the 1878 law
1908Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) ActColonial governmentAction against newspapers accused of encouraging specified offences
1910Indian Press ActColonial governmentFinancial securities and additional powers to act against publications

The Vernacular Press Act, 1878

One of the most significant measures was the Vernacular Press Act of 1878, enacted during the viceroyalty of Lord Lytton.

The law was directed at newspapers published in Indian languages rather than English. Its purpose was to control criticism of British rule in vernacular publications.

Under the Act, authorities could monitor published material and proceed against newspapers accused of producing objectionable or seditious writing. A newspaper could be warned, and further action could lead to seizure of its press and printing machinery.

Press censorship is official control over what may be published or circulated. It can involve advance scrutiny, restrictions on particular material or penalties for publication.

The Vernacular Press Act reflected colonial fears that newspapers in Indian languages were spreading criticism of government policy among a wider Indian readership.

How newspapers responded

Amrita Bazar Patrika illustrates the importance of the law's language distinction. Established in 1868 as a Bengali weekly and later published bilingually, it changed to English-only publication in 1878.

This response mattered because the 1878 Act singled out vernacular newspapers. The shift in language enabled the newspaper to avoid restrictions that applied specifically to the vernacular press.

Other editors continued to publish criticism of colonial policies despite the risk of prosecution or confiscation. Attempts to suppress the press could also increase public opposition to the government.

Repeal in 1882

The Vernacular Press Act was repealed in 1882 during the viceroyalty of Lord Ripon. This did not mean that every press restriction disappeared. Other registration requirements and legal provisions remained, and additional repressive measures were introduced in later decades.

Different purposes of the 1835 and 1867 laws

The Metcalfe Act of 1835 is remembered for relaxing earlier press licensing restrictions. It should not be confused with Macaulay's Minute on education, which was also issued in 1835.

The historical Press and Registration of Books Act of 1867 concerned the identification and registration of presses and publications. It was not the same as the Vernacular Press Act of 1878, which imposed special restrictions on the Indian-language press.

Prelims focus

  • 1823: press licensing regulations associated with John Adam.
  • 1835: Charles Metcalfe relaxed earlier press licensing restrictions.
  • 1867: Press and Registration of Books Act.
  • 1878: Vernacular Press Act under Lord Lytton.
  • 1882: repeal of the Vernacular Press Act under Lord Ripon.
  • Trap: The 1878 Act specifically targeted the vernacular press; it was not a prohibition on every English-language newspaper.

[NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, chapter Print Culture and the Modern World, section Print and Censorship, printed p. 175; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, chapter The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed pp. 109–111; Printing Presses Act, Act XI of 1835, dated 3 August 1835, sections repealing the 1823 regulations; Government of India, Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867, Act 25 of 1867, preamble and registration provisions; British Library Endangered Archives Programme, Amrita Bazar Patrika, collection EAP262/1, historical description, consulted 20 November 2026.]
